855.title: What people live by
855.hook: in Tolstoy's story an angel learns that people live by love (What Men Live By)
855.howItsDone: Tolstoy's short story What Men Live By is a moral tale; readers take from it the angel's three answers: love dwells in people, no one knows their own needs, and people live by love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simone Weil: attention is love. Your line was attention is love. Who got your five full minutes? Today, a story about a stranger who needed far more than five minutes. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

Winter, in a Russian village. A poor shoemaker named Simon is walking home with no sheepskin, because the people who owed him money didn't pay. Behind a roadside shrine he sees something pale. It's a man, naked, sitting against the wall, freezing. Simon is frightened. He walks right past. Then, a little way down the road, he stops, argues with himself, and turns back. That turn is the beginning of a short story by Leo Tolstoy called What Men Live By. Its last answer is today's word.
screen: `A POOR SHOEMAKER IN WINTER.` → `A MAN BEHIND THE SHRINE.` → `SIMON TURNS BACK.`

segments.voice: First, a stranger at the table. Simon gives the man his coat and brings him home. His wife Matryona is furious: no sheepskin, and now another mouth to feed. Then she looks at the stranger, and pity wins. She sets out bread for him. And the stranger, for the first time, smiles. He gives his name as Michael, and stays on, learning to make shoes. Second, a rich man's boots. One day a wealthy gentleman storms in and orders boots that must last a year without losing their shape. As he gives the order, Michael looks past him and smiles a second time. Then Michael makes soft slippers instead. Simon is horrified, until a servant runs back: the master has died on the way home. They need slippers for the body. Third, two little girls. One day a woman comes in with twin girls, one of them lame. Their mother died when they were born, and this neighbor took them in and raised them as her own. Michael smiles a third time. Fourth, the three answers. Michael reveals that he is an angel. He was sent to take the twins' mother's soul and refused out of pity, so he was sent to earth to learn three things. What dwells in people: love. What isn't given to people: to know their own needs, even what they'll need by evening. And what people live by. Not by careful planning for themselves, the angel says, but by love.
screen: `A STRANGER AT THE TABLE.` · `BOOTS FOR A YEAR, SLIPPERS FOR A BODY.` · `TWIN GIRLS, RAISED BY A NEIGHBOR.` · `THE THREE ANSWERS.` · then, large: `PEOPLE LIVE BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. The twins in the story lived because someone who didn't have to took them in. Look back over your own life the same way. Who fed you, taught you, drove you, sat up with you when you were sick? Let the names and faces come, one at a time, without hurrying. Some will be family. Some might surprise you: a teacher, a neighbor, a stranger at the right moment. Just notice them. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
What people live by. In Tolstoy's story, the angel's last lesson: people live not by their own planning, but by love. Today's word.
Your line: what we live by. Today, pick one person who kept you going when you couldn't manage alone, and let them know, in a sentence, that you noticed. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

options: walk on; it isn't safe.

fork.reveal: in the story, Simon does both: he's frightened and walks past, then argues with himself and turns back. the whole story begins with that turn.

what it means: three lessons about love, and about not knowing our own needs.
what a scholar hears: Tolstoy heads the story with lines on love from the first letter of John.

856.title: Goodwill for all
856.hook: Martin Luther King Jr. described agape as understanding, redeeming goodwill for all (Stride Toward Freedom)
856.howItsDone: In the nonviolent tradition Martin Luther King Jr. described, participants commit to opposing unjust deeds while seeking the good of their opponents, aiming at reconciliation rather than humiliation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tolstoy's angel learned what people live by: love. Your line was what we live by. Who did you thank for keeping you going? Today, love aimed at a hard target. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, have stopped riding the city buses. Day after day they walk to work, in the cold and the rain. Their homes are threatened. Their leaders are arrested. One of those leaders, a minister named Martin Luther King Jr., faces a hard question: how should the people feel about the ones doing this to them? Later, in a book about those days called Stride Toward Freedom, he gave his answer. He reached for an old Greek word for love, and gave it a definition. Today's word is that definition.
screen: `MONTGOMERY, ALABAMA.` → `WALKING, NOT RIDING.` → `HOW TO FEEL ABOUT OPPONENTS?`

segments.voice: First, three words for love. In Stride Toward Freedom, King lays out three Greek words. Eros, a longing, even a love of beauty. Philia, the warm love between friends, who love each other back. And agape, which is the one he means. Second, goodwill for all. King describes agape as understanding, redeeming goodwill for all people. It doesn't wait to be earned, and it doesn't ask anything back. It isn't liking. He's clear that nobody is being asked to feel affection for the person who bombed their house. Agape is a settled will for the other person's good. Third, the person, not the deed. King writes that agape loves the person who does an evil deed while hating the deed itself. That's what made his kind of nonviolence different from simply staying quiet. The boycott kept pushing. The goal, he says, was not to defeat or humiliate opponents, but to win their friendship and understanding. Fourth, an old command. King, a Baptist minister, rooted this in the Gospels, and he credited Gandhi with showing him the method. In the King James Bible, Jesus says: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." King's agape is that command, worked out in the streets of a real city, with real people on the other side.
screen: `THREE WORDS FOR LOVE.` · `UNDERSTANDING, REDEEMING GOODWILL.` · `THE PERSON, NOT THE DEED.` · `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.` · then, large: `GOODWILL FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle into a few slow breaths. Bring to mind someone you're at odds with. Not the hardest person in your life; someone medium. A coworker, a relative, a neighbor, a person whose politics drive you up the wall. You don't have to like them. Just try King's distinction: set the deed to one side, and look at the person. Then, without forcing a feeling, hold one simple wish for their good: that they're well, that they're understood. If prayer is part of your life, let the wish go there too. The bell holds the time.
Goodwill for all. Martin Luther King Jr.'s way of describing agape: understanding, redeeming goodwill, even for opponents. Today's word.
Your line: goodwill for all. Today, show one act of goodwill to someone you disagree with: a fair hearing, a courtesy, a kind word behind their back. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

match.prompt: three words for love — tap the pairs.
pairs: goodwill for all, asking nothing back

myth: King said agape means liking your opponents
he was clear it isn't liking or affection; it's goodwill for their good.
for King, agape loves the person while hating the evil deed
the person, not the deed.
King said the boycott's goal was to humiliate opponents
he said the goal was to win their friendship and understanding.

fork.setup: you're in Montgomery, and someone has threatened your home. by King's agape, what are you asked to do?
options: feel affection for them.
oppose the deed, and still will their good.
stay quiet and stop the boycott.
fork.reveal: agape isn't liking and isn't silence: the boycott kept pushing, while aiming to win the opponent's understanding.

original.note: Greek: the love King described as understanding, redeeming goodwill for all.

trapdoor: what you thought: agape is just a fancy word for love.
what it means: a settled goodwill that seeks even an opponent's good.
what a scholar hears: King sets agape beside eros and philia, and grounds it in love your enemies.

sources.ref: Martin Luther King Jr., Stride Toward Freedom, chapter on the pilgrimage to nonviolence

857.title: It grows
857.hook: a study tested whether weeks of loving-kindness practice change a person's days
857.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators practice loving-kindness (metta) by silently wishing well to themselves and others in widening circles, often for a set time each day; the practice is also taught in secular meditation courses and has been studied by psychologists.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin Luther King Jr. on agape. Your line was goodwill for all. Did an opponent get a little of it? Today, a question for the lab: can that kind of love be practiced into being? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

May all beings be happy. That's the heart of an old Buddhist teaching, the Metta Sutta, which describes a love meant to reach every living thing, near and far, seen and unseen. Say a sentence like that, and a fair question comes up. Does saying it change anything in the one who says it? Or is it a lovely sentence that floats away? A team of psychologists decided to find out. They taught a group of working adults a loving-kindness meditation, then followed them week after week, asking each evening how the day had gone inside. Today: what they found, and why the title is only two words.
screen: `MAY ALL BEINGS BE HAPPY.` → `DOES SAYING IT CHANGE ANYTHING?` → `A TEAM DECIDED TO FIND OUT.`

segments.voice: First, a practice, not a mood. In the Metta Sutta, boundless love isn't something that simply happens to a person. The text speaks of cultivating a boundless heart toward all beings, the way a mother guards her only child. Buddhist teachers call metta a practice: you sit, you bring someone to mind, and you wish them well on purpose, whether or not the warmth shows up. Second, the study. Psychologist Barbara Fredrickson and her colleagues ran it. Some participants learned loving-kindness meditation; a comparison group waited their turn for the course. Both groups kept reporting on their days. Over the weeks, the meditators reported more positive emotions in ordinary life, things like joy, gratitude, contentment, hope and love. Third, small days, stacked up. The gains didn't arrive all at once on day one. The paper describes them showing up gradually, as people kept practicing. That's the plain meaning of today's line. Nobody flipped a switch. Something got watered. Fourth, what it built. Fredrickson's larger idea is called broaden and build: good feelings widen what a person notices, and over time they build lasting resources. In the study, the meditators also reported more sense of purpose, more support from others, and more satisfaction with their lives. Now the honest part. This is one study. People reported on themselves, and the changes were modest. It doesn't prove anything about the deep nature of love. But on one plain point it agrees with the old sutta: this kind of love is something a person can grow.
screen: `A PRACTICE, NOT A MOOD.` · `THE STUDY: WEEKS, NOT MOMENTS.` · `SMALL DAYS, STACKED UP.` · `WHAT IT BUILT.` · then, large: `IT GROWS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone easy to love: a friend, a grandparent, a pet. Silently offer them the kind of wish the practice uses, something like may you be well, may you be at ease. Let the words go slowly. If warmth comes, fine. If it doesn't, keep going anyway; that's the practice. Stay with this one person the whole time, repeating the wish at the pace of the breath, the way a gardener waters the same bed every day. If you pray, you can hold them before God as you go. The bell holds the time.
It grows. Loving-kindness treated as a practice that strengthens with use, as the Metta Sutta teaches and a modern study set out to test. Today's word.
Your line: it grows. Today, find five minutes for loving-kindness somewhere in the day, and check one thing at the end: was it any easier than at the start? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

pairs: a Buddhist text on boundless love
good feelings widen and build resources

myth: in the study, the gains arrived on the first day and then stayed flat
they showed up gradually as people kept practicing.
the comparison group waited their turn for the course
they were a waiting group, so the two could be compared.
the study proved that love is the deepest truth of the universe

fork.setup: you've just started a loving-kindness course. week one, and it feels like nothing. what do you do?
options: quit: it clearly doesn't work for you.
keep practicing, a little, day after day.
sit for hours once, to force it.
fork.reveal: in the study the gains came gradually, over weeks of practice. that's the title: it grows.

original.note: metta, the Pali word for loving-kindness, from the Buddhist tradition.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving-kindness is a feeling you either have or don't.
what it means: it's a practice, and it can strengthen with use.
what a scholar hears: the Metta Sutta speaks of cultivating boundless love, and a modern study with a waiting comparison group reported positive emotions rising gradually with practice.

sources.ref: Fredrickson, Cohn, Coffey, Pek & Finkel, "Open Hearts Build Lives," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 95(5)

858.title: The difficult
858.hook: love isn't only for the easy ones
858.howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness practice, people often wish well to themselves, a friend and a neutral person before turning to someone difficult; Jews and Christians read Proverbs 25 on feeding a hungry enemy as practical guidance; Stoics prepare in the morning for the people they will meet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a study of loving-kindness. Your line was it grows. Did five minutes feel any easier by the end? Today, the hardest ground to grow it in. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

"Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." That's how a Roman emperor, Marcus Aurelius, opens the second book of his private notebook. Not a pep talk. A weather report. He ran an empire, and he knew the day would include people who were hard to be around. So do the rest of us: a coworker who takes credit, a relative who knows exactly which button to press, a neighbor with a leaf blower and opinions. Loving the easy ones takes no training at all. Today: three old voices on the other ones.
screen: `BEGIN THE MORNING BY SAYING TO THYSELF.` → `A WEATHER REPORT.` → `THE OTHER ONES.`

segments.voice: First, the emperor's warning. Marcus doesn't stop at the list. He goes on to say that these people act as they do because they don't know what is good and bad. None of them can make him do wrong, so none of them can really injure him, and he can't hate them, because they are his kin. Then he says something surprising for an emperor: we are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids. To work against each other is against nature. Second, bread for an enemy. The book of Proverbs puts it in kitchen terms: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." Nothing there about warm feelings. The proverb asks for bread and water, handed to someone who wishes you harm. Third, the hard one comes last. In the Path of Purification, the Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa gives an order for loving-kindness practice. Begin with yourself. Then a dear friend. Then someone neutral. Only then someone hostile. He warns against starting with the hostile person, because resentment comes up first. In other words, he doesn't pretend it's easy; he builds a ramp. Fourth, well-wishing isn't trusting. None of these voices asks anyone to hand a difficult person the car keys. Wishing someone well can sit alongside a locked door, a firm no, a boundary kept. It means hoping they find their way to being well, from a safe distance if need be. The hard ones too. Not first, not instead of safety, but too.
screen: `THE EMPEROR'S MORNING WARNING.` · `BREAD FOR AN ENEMY.` · `THE HARD ONE COMES LAST.` · `WELL-WISHING ISN'T TRUSTING.` · then, large: `THE HARD ONES TOO.`

segments.voice: Use Buddhaghosa's ramp. Start with yourself: may I be well. Then a friend, for a few breaths. Then someone neutral, a face from the store. Only now, gently, the fourth step: someone mildly difficult, a person who simply irritates you. Hold them in mind and offer the same wish: may you be well. If resentment comes up, notice it, and go back to the friend for a breath, then try again. If you pray, you can name them before God. The bell holds the time.
The difficult. The people who are hard to love, whom Marcus expected each morning, Proverbs says to feed anyway, and Buddhaghosa placed last on the ramp. Today's word.
Your line: the hard ones too. Today, when a difficult person crosses your path, wish them well silently once, and keep whatever boundary you need. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

pairs: bread and water for an enemy

he starts with yourself and warns against starting with a hostile person.
Marcus Aurelius said we are made for cooperation, like hands and feet
he says working against each other is against nature.
wishing a difficult person well means you have to trust them again

fork.setup: you're starting loving-kindness practice for the first time. where do you begin?
options: with the person who hurt you most.
with yourself, then a friend.
with a crowd of strangers.
fork.reveal: Buddhaghosa's order starts with yourself, then a dear friend, then someone neutral, and the hostile person last.

trapdoor: what you thought: love is for the people who are easy to love.
what it means: several traditions train it toward difficult people too, without giving up safety.
what a scholar hears: Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification sets an order for metta practice that leaves the hostile person until last, a ramp rather than a leap.

859.title: Your own body
859.hook: several traditions honor the body as gift or temple
859.howItsDone: Some Christians speak of the body as a temple, after Paul's letter to the Corinthians; Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, including the praise of being wonderfully made; Buddhists tell how the Buddha left behind extreme fasting and took food before his awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the difficult people. Your line was the hard ones too. Did a quiet wish go to someone hard? Today, a closer neighbor than any of them: the one you live inside. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

Knees that click on the stairs. A back that votes against getting out of bed. A face under the bathroom light at seven in the morning. For some people, the harshest words of the whole day are never said out loud. They're said silently, to their own body. Meanwhile that same body has been breathing all night without being asked, healing a paper cut nobody thanked it for, and carrying its owner to the bathroom mirror to be criticized. This block of the path is about love. Today it turns to the one thing anyone hearing this is living in.
screen: `KNEES THAT CLICK ON THE STAIRS.` → `WORDS SAID SILENTLY TO A BODY.` → `BREATHING ALL NIGHT, UNTHANKED.`

segments.voice: First, fearfully and wonderfully made. In the Psalms, a singer looks at their own body and starts praising: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Not perfectly made. Not admired by others. Wonderfully made, with a little awe mixed in. In that psalm, the body is a gift and a wonder before it's anything else. Second, a temple, not a project. Writing to Christians in Corinth who were arguing about what they could do with their bodies, Paul asks: "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you". In context, Paul is warning them about how they use their bodies, and the image he picks raises the stakes: a temple is holy, a place where God dwells, not something to use carelessly. Third, the Buddha accepts a meal. In a sutta in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha remembers his life before awakening. He tried to wring freedom out of his body by starving it, until it was skin and bone. It didn't work. Then he remembered sitting peacefully under a tree as a boy, and he asked whether that kind of ease was really something to fear. He decided it wasn't, and he took solid food again. In the story, the way forward began with a meal. Fourth, kind, not perfect. None of these texts asks for a body that looks a certain way. They ask for something smaller: reverence, care, an end to treating it as an enemy. Sleep when it's tired. Feed it. Stop the silent insults for one day. This body, as it is.
screen: `FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.` · `A TEMPLE, NOT A PROJECT.` · `THE BUDDHA ACCEPTS A MEAL.` · `KIND, NOT PERFECT.` · then, large: `THIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whatever is kind to your back right now. Start at the feet. Feel them, and silently thank them for today's steps. Move up slowly: legs, belly, hands, shoulders, the face. Wherever there's an ache, don't argue with it; just rest your attention there for a breath, the way you'd sit with a friend who's tired. If the old critical words show up, let them pass and go back to thanks. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for this body. The bell holds the time.
Your own body. Something the Psalms call wonderfully made, Paul calls a temple, and the Buddha's story says should be fed, not starved. Today's word.
Your line: this body. Today, do one kind thing for it on purpose: a glass of water, a real lunch, a walk, an earlier night. And catch one silent insult before it lands. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

pairs: left starving behind and ate again
holy, not something to use carelessly

it says fearfully and wonderfully made.
in the sutta, the Buddha's starving brought him to awakening
it didn't work; he took solid food again.

fork.setup: you're the young seeker. a long stretch of starving has left you skin and bone, and no closer to freedom. what do you do?
options: fast harder; it must be working.
eat a real meal and keep going.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving your body means liking how it looks.

what a scholar hears: in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha's path turns when he gives up self-starvation and eats, so care for the body sits inside the story of awakening.

860.title: Loving a partner
860.hook: love as daily choice, not only feeling
860.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the Song of Songs as a love poem and as a picture of love between God and people; Christians read Paul's words on love in 1 Corinthians 13, sometimes at weddings; some couples, religious or not, describe their commitment as something renewed in small daily acts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your own body. Your line was this body. Did it get one kind thing on purpose, a glass of water or an earlier night? Today, from the body to the person who shares the days. Day eight hundred sixty.

English has a strange phrase for the start of love. People fall into it. Falling is something that happens to you: no plan, no effort, just gravity. And that's a fine way to begin. But nobody falls into doing the dishes at eleven at night so the other person can sleep. Nobody falls into listening to the same work story for the third time with real interest. Those things are done on purpose, on ordinary days, when the feeling is quiet. Today: an old song, an old letter and a modern book, all asking the same question. What is love once the falling is over?
screen: `PEOPLE FALL INTO IT.` → `NOBODY FALLS INTO THE DISHES.` → `ONCE THE FALLING IS OVER.`

segments.voice: First, the song. The Song of Songs in the Hebrew Bible is a long love poem, full of gardens and longing, and near its end it says: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." Some Jewish and Christian readers take the Song as a picture of love between God and people; others read it as a song about two lovers. Either way, the claim is about endurance: real love survives the flood. Second, the letter. Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, describes love in the King James wording as charity: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind." Notice the verbs. Suffering long. Being kind. Not envying. Paul isn't describing a feeling that washes over someone. He's describing how a person behaves, especially when it's hard. Third, the book. The psychoanalyst Erich Fromm, in The Art of Loving, argued that love is an art, something learned and practiced, and that loving someone is more than a strong feeling. He called it a decision, a judgment and a promise. A feeling, he pointed out, can come and go; a promise can be kept on the days the feeling is away. Fourth, small choices, daily. None of these voices says feelings don't matter. They say feelings aren't the whole of it. Love between partners lives in small acts: a coffee made the way the other person likes it, a phone put face down, an apology offered first. One more honest word: choosing love daily never means choosing to stay where you're harmed. A daily choice is made freely, by both.
screen: `MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE.` · `CHARITY SUFFERETH LONG.` · `A DECISION, A PROMISE.` · `SMALL CHOICES, DAILY.` · then, large: `A DAILY CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Let a partner come to mind. If there isn't one right now, choose anyone you've decided to love: a sibling, a close friend, a parent. Breathe slowly and hold their face. Ask yourself quietly: what small thing would make their day a little lighter? Not a grand gesture. Something they'd notice. Let one answer settle. Then, for the rest of the sit, simply wish them well, and picture yourself doing that small thing later today. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Loving a partner. Love kept up on ordinary days, the long-suffering kindness Paul describes and the decision and promise Fromm wrote about. Today's word.
Your line: a daily choice. Today, do the one small thing you chose for your partner or the person you love, without announcing it. Day eight hundred sixty.

the Song of Songs has been read both as a love poem and as a picture of God and people

options: wait until you feel like it.

fork.reveal: Fromm's point: a promise can be kept on the days the feeling is away. love shows up in the small act.

original.note: ahavah, the Hebrew word for love in the Song of Songs: many waters cannot quench it.

trapdoor: what you thought: love is a feeling you fall into, or out of.
what it means: it's also a choice, made again on ordinary days.
what a scholar hears: the King James 'charity' in 1 Corinthians 13 is described entirely through what love does and doesn't do, and Fromm called love a decision, a judgment and a promise.

sources.ref: Erich Fromm, The Art of Loving, ch. 2

861.title: Friendship kept up
861.howItsDone: In Jewish and Christian tradition, Proverbs is read as practical wisdom about friendship; people keep friendships alive through visits, calls, letters and shared meals, sometimes around holidays and life events.

segments.voice: Yesterday, loving a partner. Your line was a daily choice. Did the small thing get done, without announcing it? Today, the week's last day, and the love that has no anniversary to remind anyone. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

Somewhere in a phone there's a name that used to be a daily call. Nobody fought. Nobody decided anything. One of you moved, or had a baby, or changed jobs, and the calls became texts, and the texts became birthday messages, and then one year even the birthday slipped by. Sometimes a friendship doesn't end with a slammed door at all. It ends like a houseplant on a high shelf: not killed, just not watered. Marriages have vows and anniversaries. Families have holidays. Friendship mostly has nothing holding it up except the people in it. Today: three old lines about keeping it alive.
screen: `A NAME THAT USED TO BE A DAILY CALL.` → `NOBODY DECIDED ANYTHING.` → `A HOUSEPLANT ON A HIGH SHELF.`

segments.voice: First, Proverbs on the old friend. "Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not." Look at the second half. Not just your friend, but your father's friend: someone you inherited. The book of Proverbs treats an old friendship as something worth keeping across a lifetime, even passed down like a family table. Second, shew himself friendly. Another proverb, in the King James wording: "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly." Having friends and showing friendliness are tied together. The friendship doesn't run on its own. Someone has to keep showing up. Third, to have a friend, be one. Ralph Waldo Emerson, in his essay on friendship, puts it in one line: "The only way to have a friend is to be one." Emerson can be lofty about friendship, but this line is practical. It moves the question from whether they've called lately to whether you have. Fourth, small, often, on purpose. Tending a friendship isn't a big reunion trip. It's a short message that says I thought of you. A photo of the café you both used to sit in. A question about their mother's surgery.
